entries.title: Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
entries.summary: Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.
entries.content:
November 17, 2026

Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany. 

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

entries.title: United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights
entries.summary: United Airlines said a system outage that delayed departures has been resolved. The disruption came on the heels of a stoppage that halted all flights to and across the US for five hours last week.
entries.content:
United States of America

United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights

November 17, 2026

United Airlines said a system outage that delayed departures has been resolved. The disruption came on the heels of a stoppage that halted all flights to and across the US for five hours last week.

United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" that affected hundreds of departing flights on Monday.

Flight tracker FlightAware said 418 United flights were delayed on Monday afternoon.

The issue comes three days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network grounded flights across the US on Friday.

What did United Airlines say about Monday's tech issues?

United Airlines said there was "no indication" that Monday's outage was the result of a cyberattack.

There was also no indication that the issues affecting United Airlines on Monday were related to Friday's nationwide shutdown.

United Airlines said later on Monday that it had "resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures."

The airline added that airborne flights, as well as those operated by its regional brand United Express, were not affected.

The disruption on Friday and Monday highlights how vulnerable air travel is to tech failures.

Disruption follows other recent major tech meltdowns

United Airlines' computer problem comes amid other recent similar high-profile technology meltdowns, including Friday's nationwide grounding.

Thousands of people in the US said they were unable to access their online banking accounts at several large US banks after JPMorgan Chase reported a technical issue.

On Thursday, Microsoft saw a major disruption to its services, including its Outlook email and Teams messenger. 

The tech company said Saturday that its services had been fully restored.

entries.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
entries.summary: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.
entries.content:
November 16, 2026

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Son of boxer, head of French football

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was appointed the federation's president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Embattled Infantino

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

entries.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
entries.summary: Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.
entries.content:
Europe

EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman

November 16, 2026

Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.

The European Union added Russia's wealthiest woman, online retailer Wildberries' CEO and owner Tatyana Kim, to its Russian sanctions list on Monday.

Kim's EU assets will be frozen as a result and she is barred from making financial transactions in or traveling to the bloc.

Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce retailer.

Kim, born in Grozny, Chechnya, to ethnic Korean parents, has an estimated net worth of $8.1 billion (€7.4 billion).

The sanctions were part of a larger regime targeting some 50 banks and oil export enablers and nearly 100 business leaders, propagandists and a major pro-Russian hacking group.

EU authorities say they targeted ​Kim due to the fact that Wildberries is "one of the largest taxpayers" in Russia and "operates as a supply network ​for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and ​dual-use ‌goods."

An EU statement went on to say that "Kim is supporting, materially or financially, and benefiting from Russia's military and industrial complex."

Why is the EU targeting an online retailer?

In its defense against invading Russian forces, Ukraine expanded its military target list this summer to include Wildberries warehouses inside Russia, saying the company's product list — which includes night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets alongside ‌regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics — is supporting Russia's illegal war.

Kim defended her company at the time, saying its offerings were no different than other online retailers like Amazon in the US and Alibaba in China.

The Kremlin, too, denied that the company and its warehouses were involved in the war effort.

Who else is on the EU's newest sanctions list?

In a statement, Wildberries said Brussels' sanctions would have no impact on the company since it has no assets in the bloc nor does it conduct business there.

Other entities on Monday's sanctions list include firms in China, Oman, the Seychelles and the United Arab Emirates linked to the sale of oil from Russia's so-called shadow fleet of illicit tankers.

The sale of that oil also fuels Russia's invasion, which the EU is seeking to hamper through sanctions as well as direct financial and military assistance for Kyiv.

Brussels has imposed more than 20 sanctions packages in response to Russia's February 24, 2022, invasion of Ukraine, targeting thousands of individuals and companies to pressure President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the assault.

The 27-nation bloc intends to introduce another sweeping sanctions package by year's end.

entries.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
entries.summary: Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care

November 16, 2026

Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed to the country's Supreme Court in a bid to receive urgent medical attention for himself and his wife.

According to an open letter conveyed to the court through Khan's lawyer, the former leader's doctors had warned him of a risk for brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that his blood pressure had risen sharply.

He also said his wife Bushra Bibi required further eye operation, and that she is at risk of losing her eyesight should she not be granted the surgery.

The letter was released to the public by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar.

"Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” the letter reads, asking the judges to give him "justice" before it was too late.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," Khan wrote.

Government contests account

An earlier court order ordered Khan's transfer to a hospital in Pakistani capital Islamabad, with Khan alleging that the authorities had not implemented it.

However, cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan was receiving medical care, while also receiving food and books of his liking.

According to Chaudhry, the former leader has been taken to medical examinations at a hospital in Islamabad eight times, with his health and blood pressure being found to be in order.

Still a popular figure

Despite being in prison since 2023 for corruption offenses, Khan is still considered a popular figure in Pakistan, with his party demanding his release. His wife is alo serving jail time for graft offenses.

Khan argues the charges against him are politically motivated, which the government denies.

The government, led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, also denied Khan was in solitary confinement. More than 900 visits to Khan have been registered since he started his jail time in 2023, according to the authorities.

In a previous case, Khan's attorney told the court that his client had lost about 85% of his right eye's vision. However, his sister later said his situation was improving.

entries.title: Grammy Awards: Raye and Rosalia lead nominations
entries.summary: The nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards are in and women dominated the top categories for the highest accolade in the music industry.
entries.content:
November 16, 2026

The nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards are in and women dominated the top categories for the highest accolade in the music industry.

British singer Raye, with the genre mixing hit "Where Is My Husband!," landed at the top of the list of Grammy Award nominees on Monday, followed by Spanish musician Rosalia and "Choosin" Texas" artist Ella ‌Langley.

Raye earned 11 ⁠Grammy ⁠nominations including nods for song and record of the year for "Husband," and for album of the year for "This Music May Contain Hope."

She now ties Beyonce's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.

For her part, Rosalia received nine nominations, just days after sweeping the Latin Grammys with ​her album "Lux."

First-time nominee Langley secured seven, as did Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers.

Megastar Taylor Swift received five nominations.

Only one male artist nominated for Best Album

Besides Raye, competitors in the album race include Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl," Langley's "Dandelion," Rosalia's "Lux," Bridgers' "Lost Weekend," Olivia Dean's "The Art of Loving," and Rodrigo's "you ​seem pretty sad for a girl so in love." Bruno Mars was the only male artist nominated in the category, for his album "The Romantic."

The record of the year category is made up of Dean's “Man I Need,” Langley's “Choosin' Texas,” Mars' “I Just Might,” Raye's “Where Is My Husband!”, Rodrigo's “The Cure,” Rosalía’s “Berghain” featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia” and Tame Impala and Jennie's “Dracula.”

K-pop sensation ⁠BTS declined to submit any ​music for consideration in protest over a new Asian pop music category. Members of the South Korean band said they did not believe music should be categorized by region.

Dolly Parton, the country legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.

Winners will be announced on February

The final Grammy voting round will run from December 10 to January 7, with winners selected by around 16,000 Recording Academy members.

Winners will be announced at a red-carpet ceremony in downtown Los Angeles ‌on ​February 7.

The event will be broadcast live on Walt Disney's ABC and streamed on Disney+ and Hulu.

entries.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
entries.summary: When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.
entries.content:
November 16, 2026

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it. 

Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

entries.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
entries.summary: In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

November 16, 2026

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

How it all started

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

A machismo problem

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Questionable lifestyle choices

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

Why are all secretaries women?

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

Inappropriate casting

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Pattinson as a modern 007?

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

entries.title: Nvidia scandal: China's chips dilemma, US rivalry shape AI race
entries.summary: The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.
entries.content:
November 16, 2026

The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.

China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.   

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.

The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.

But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.

US moves to restrict China's access to chips

As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.

Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."

US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.

Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week, enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.

Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trumpduring his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.

In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.

Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series, it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.

Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.

Nvidia affair and espionage allegations

But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.

The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.

Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.

China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.

Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.

"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.

It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."

Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.

A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"

Behind the verbal sparring lies an economic calculation.

Is China buying more US chips?

Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.

Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.

The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.

For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."

Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.

"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.

This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.

According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.

China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.

"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.

China lacks advanced chip-making equipment

However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.

Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.

Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.

The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."

According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."

Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Tesla planning €3BN investment in German factory to produce Cybercabs
entries.summary: The Elon Musk-owned company is looking to further expand its only European production line. Brandenburg's state leader has welcomed the decision.
